extracted.intended_audience: ICLR 2024 reviewers (peer reviewers for the ICLR conference)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines for performing peer review of submissions to ICLR 2024, including step-by-step reviewer tasks, ethical reporting, review structure, discussion participation, and decision criteria.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timely and substantive reviews
rubrics_metrics.description: Your reviews are timely and substantive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reviews should be submitted within the conference timeline (see main reviewer tasks/dates). Timeliness is emphasized as a core expectation and is tied to recognition (top reviewers acknowledged).

rubrics_metrics.name: Read the paper thoroughly
rubrics_metrics.description: It’s important to carefully read through the entire paper, and to look up any related work and citations that will help you comprehensively evaluate it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Give yourself sufficient time. Consider reading related literature to judge novelty, correctness, and placement in the literature; consult supplementary material if necessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify objective of the work
rubrics_metrics.description: While reading, consider the following: Objective of the work: What is the goal of the paper? Is it to better address a known application or problem, draw attention to a new application or problem, or to introduce and/or explain a new theoretical finding? A combination of these?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Different objectives require different considerations as to potential value and impact; explicitly identify the paper's objective to inform your evaluation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluate strengths (quality dimensions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Strong points: is the submission clear, technically correct, experimentally rigorous, reproducible, does it present novel findings (e.g., theoretically, algorithmically, etc.)?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for clarity of presentation, correctness of proofs/derivations, rigor of experiments (statistical significance, baselines, ablations), and whether the work advances knowledge or methods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluate weaknesses across same dimensions
rubrics_metrics.description: Weak points: is it weak in any of the aspects listed in b.?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicitly list weaknesses in clarity, correctness, experimental support, reproducibility, novelty claims, assumptions, or scope. Be comprehensive and specific.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid and be mindful of biases
rubrics_metrics.description: Be mindful of potential biases and try to be open-minded about the value and interest a paper can hold for the entire ICLR community, even if it may not be very interesting for you.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate work on community value and scientific merits rather than personal taste; avoid dismissing work solely because it is outside your immediate interests.

rubrics_metrics.name: Answer four key decision questions
rubrics_metrics.description: Answer four key questions for yourself, to make a recommendation to Accept or Reject: (1) What is the specific question and/or problem tackled by the paper? (2) Is the approach well motivated, including being well-placed in the literature? (3) Does the paper support the claims? This includes determining if results, whether theoretical or empirical, are correct and if they are scientifically rigorous. (4) What is the significance of the work? Does it contribute new knowledge and sufficient value to the community?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these four questions jointly to form your accept/reject recommendation. Note significance does not require state-of-the-art performance; value may be empirical, theoretical, or practical.

rubrics_metrics.name: Initial review: structure and content
rubrics_metrics.description: Write and submit your initial review, organizing it as follows: Summarize what the paper claims to contribute. Be positive and constructive. List strong and weak points of the paper. Be as comprehensive as possible. Clearly state your initial recommendation (accept or reject) with one or two key reasons for this choice. Provide supporting arguments for your recommendation. Ask questions you would like answered by the authors to help you clarify your understanding of the paper and provide the additional evidence you need to be confident in your assessment. Provide additional feedback with the aim to improve the paper.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Structure reviews to help area chairs and authors quickly understand the contribution, rationale for the score, and concrete ways to improve. Make clear which feedback is for improvement vs. which affects the accept/reject decision.

rubrics_metrics.name: Complete the Code of Ethics (CoE) report
rubrics_metrics.description: Complete the CoE report: ICLR has adopted the Code of Ethics. When submitting your review, you’ll be asked to complete a CoE report for the paper. The report is a simple form with two questions. The first asks whether there is a potential violation of the CoE. The second is relevant only if there is a potential violation and asks the reviewer to explain why there may be a potential violation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Read the Code of Ethics before reviewing. If you suspect a violation, indicate it in the CoE report; ACs/PCs/ethics board will handle cases. For other policy violations (plagiarism, double submission, formatting), use confidential comments to AC/SAC/PC.

rubrics_metrics.name: Engage actively in discussion phase
rubrics_metrics.description: Engage in discussion: reviewers, authors and area chairs engage in asynchronous discussion and authors are allowed to revise their submissions to address concerns that arise. It is crucial that you are actively engaged during this phase.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be open to changing your initial recommendation (either more positive or more negative). Read author replies and other reviewers’ comments, ask clarifying questions, and use new information to update your assessment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Borderline paper meeting expectations
rubrics_metrics.description: Borderline paper meeting: ACs are encouraged to (virtually) meet and discuss with reviewers only for borderline cases. ACs will schedule the meeting and facilitate the discussion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Familiarize yourself with other reviewers' feedback prior to the meeting. Attend if possible; reviewers who fail to attend may have their inputs considered differently (excluding emergencies).

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide final recommendation after discussion
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide final recommendation: Update your review, taking into account the new information collected during the discussion phase, and any revisions to the submission. State your reasoning and what did/didn’t change your recommendation throughout the discussion phase.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicitly note what evidence led you to change (or not change) your view; ensure final recommendation is justified by the paper and discussion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of supplementary material
rubrics_metrics.description: How should I use supplementary material? It is not necessary to read supplementary material but such material can often answer questions that arise while reading the main paper, so consider looking there before asking authors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consult appendices/supplementary files when they contain proofs, experimental details, or additional results that bear on your evaluation or questions for authors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requesting additional experiments policy
rubrics_metrics.description: Am I allowed to ask for additional experiments? You can ask for additional experiments. New experiments should not significantly change the content of the submission. Rather, they should be limited in scope and serve to more thoroughly validate existing results from the submission.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Requests for experiments should aim to validate or probe existing claims (e.g., ablations, additional baselines) and avoid asking for a major extension or fundamentally new direction.

rubrics_metrics.name: State-of-the-art is not required
rubrics_metrics.description: If a submission does not achieve state-of-the-art results, is that grounds for rejection? No, a lack of state-of-the-art results does not by itself constitute grounds for rejection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether the submission convincingly demonstrates new, relevant, impactful knowledge even if it does not outperform prior art on benchmarks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expectations on citing and comparing with very recent work
rubrics_metrics.description: Are authors expected to cite and compare with very recent work? We consider papers contemporaneous if they are published (available in online proceedings) within the last four months. Authors are encouraged to cite and discuss all relevant papers, but they may be excused for not knowing about papers not published in peer-reviewed conference proceedings or journals, which includes papers exclusively available on arXiv.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reviewers should use good judgement; if in doubt about contemporaneous work or comparisons, discuss with the area chair rather than penalizing authors for missing very recent publications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be constructive and kind
rubrics_metrics.description: Summarize what the paper claims to contribute. Be positive and constructive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criticize with the goal of helping authors improve; separate improvement suggestions from accept/reject rationale; use respectful, professional language (see Code of Conduct).

rubrics_metrics.name: Check technical claims and experimental validity in detail
rubrics_metrics.description: Does the paper support the claims? This includes determining if results, whether theoretical or empirical, are correct and if they are scientifically rigorous.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Verify mathematical derivations and assumptions where feasible; check experiments for adequate baselines, hyperparameter tuning, number of runs/statistical significance, appropriate metrics, and clear descriptions of protocols. Ask for clarifications when details are missing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assess novelty and relation to prior work
rubrics_metrics.description: Is the approach well motivated, including being well-placed in the literature?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether claimed theorems/techniques are novel relative to cited prior work; request clearer novelty statements or literature comparisons if needed; be wary of over-claims.
